title: The Norm of Who Gets to Advocate in Team Discussions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that the best leaders don't let team norms emerge organically over time; they import and declare useful norms directly, then hold the team accountable for enforcing them. It highlights one norm as especially consequential: who gets airtime in meetings. Left unaddressed, status and seniority tend to determine whose ideas get heard, sidelining genuine expertise. The author proposes an explicit norm guaranteeing that anyone with relevant expertise or a strong viewpoint gets uninterrupted floor time, arguing this single change distinguishes the highest-performing teams.
points: Waiting for team norms to develop naturally is slow and risks entrenching dysfunctional habits.
The best leaders declare norms outright and hold team members accountable to each other for enforcing them.
Left unmanaged, status and seniority often determine who gets heard in meetings, not the quality of the idea.
An explicit norm giving genuine expertise the floor is proposed as a marker of high-performing teams.
quotes: Norms are shared agreements among team members about which behaviors are valued in the team and which behaviors are not.
Leaving it to the team and its natural process to create norms not only takes too much time, but can also result in dysfunctional norms.
How vigorously a team enforces a norm typically reflects how important they perceive it is to the leader.
A common norm on many teams is to give leaders and those with higher status more airtime.
Anyone with expertise or a strong viewpoint who wants to be heard on a topic will be given the floor and allowed to articulate their views without interruption or disagreement.
